# sp_trie - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sp-trie/

## Expand description

Utility functions to interact with Substrate’s Base-16 Modified Merkle Patricia tree (“trie”).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [accessed_](https://docs.rs/accessed_nodes_tracker/index.html)- nodes_ - tracker
- Helpers for checking for duplicate nodes.
- [cache](https://docs.rs/cache/index.html)
- Trie Cache
- [nibble_](https://docs.rs/nibble_ops/index.html)- ops
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Utility methods to work on radix 16 nibble.
- [proof_](https://docs.rs/proof_size_extension/index.html)- size_ - extension
- Externalities extension that provides access to the current proof size of the underlying recorder.
- [recorder](https://docs.rs/recorder/index.html)
- Trie recorder
- [recorder_](https://docs.rs/recorder_ext/index.html)- ext
- Extension for the default recorder.
- [trie_](https://docs.rs/trie_types/index.html)- types
- This module is for non generic definition of trie type.
Only the `Hasher`trait is generic in this case.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.CompactProof.html)- Proof
- Storage proof in compact form.
- [HashKey](https://docs.rs/struct.HashKey.html)
- Various re-exports from the `memory-db`crate. Key function that only uses the hash
- [KeySpacedDB](https://docs.rs/struct.KeySpacedDB.html)
- `HashDB`implementation that append a encoded prefix (unique id bytes) in addition to the prefix of every key value.
- [KeySpacedDB](https://docs.rs/struct.KeySpacedDBMut.html)- Mut
- `HashDBMut`implementation that append a encoded prefix (unique id bytes) in addition to the prefix of every key value.
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/struct.LayoutV0.html)- V0
- substrate trie layout
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/struct.LayoutV1.html)- V1
- substrate trie layout, with external value nodes.
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeCodec.html)- Codec
- The Substrate format implementation of `NodeCodec`. Concrete implementation of a`NodeCodecT`
- [Prefixed](https://docs.rs/struct.PrefixedKey.html)- Key
- Various re-exports from the `memory-db`crate. Key function that concatenates prefix and hash.
- [Random](https://docs.rs/struct.RandomState.html)- State
- `RandomState`is the default state for- `HashMap`
- [Recorder](https://docs.rs/struct.Recorder.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Records trie nodes as they pass it.
- [Storage](https://docs.rs/struct.StorageProof.html)- Proof
- A proof that some set of key-value pairs are included in the storage trie. The proof contains the storage values so that the partial storage backend can be reconstructed by a verifier that does not already have access to the key-value pairs.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBDoubleEndedIterator.html)- Double - Ended - Iterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Double ended iterator for going through all values in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBIterator.html)- Iterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Iterator for going through all values in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBKeyDoubleEndedIterator.html)- KeyDouble - Ended - Iterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Double ended iterator for going through all of key with values in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBKeyIterator.html)- KeyIterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Iterator for going through all of key with values in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBNodeDoubleEndedIterator.html)- Node - Double - Ended - Iterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Double ended iterator for going through all nodes in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieDBRawIterator.html)- RawIterator
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Iterator for going through all nodes in the trie in pre-order traversal order.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/struct.TrieStream.html)- Stream
- The Substrate format implementation of `TrieStream`. Codec-flavored TrieStream.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Compact](https://docs.rs/enum.CompactProofError.html)- Proof - Error
- Trie codec reexport, mainly child trie support for trie compact proof. Error for trie node decoding.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Our `NodeCodec`-specific error. Error type used for trie related errors.
- [Merkle](https://docs.rs/enum.MerkleValue.html)- Value
- Either the `hash`or`value`of a node depending on its size.
- [Node](https://docs.rs/enum.NodePlan.html)- Plan
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. A`NodePlan`is a blueprint for decoding a node from a byte slice. The`NodePlan`is created by parsing an encoded node and can be reused multiple times. This is useful as a`Node`borrows from a byte slice and this struct does not.
- [Storage](https://docs.rs/enum.StorageProofError.html)- Proof - Error
- Error associated with the `storage_proof`module.
- [Value](https://docs.rs/enum.ValuePlan.html)- Plan
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Plan for value representation in`NodePlan`.
- [Verify](https://docs.rs/enum.VerifyError.html)- Error
- Errors that may occur during proof verification. Most of the errors types simply indicate that the proof is invalid with respect to the statement being verified, and the exact error type can be used for debugging.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [EMPTY_](https://docs.rs/static.EMPTY_PREFIX.html)- PREFIX
- Various re-exports from the `hash-db`crate. An empty prefix constant. Can be use when the prefix is not use internally or for root nodes.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsHashDB](https://docs.rs/trait.AsHashDB.html)
- Reexport from `hash_db`, with genericity set for`Hasher`trait.
- [HashDBT](https://docs.rs/trait.HashDBT.html)
- Various re-exports from the `hash-db`crate. Trait modelling datastore keyed by a hash defined by the`Hasher`.
- [KeyFunction](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyFunction.html)
- Various re-exports from the `memory-db`crate.
- [Proof](https://docs.rs/trait.ProofSizeProvider.html)- Size - Provider
- Type that is able to provide a proof size estimation.
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.Query.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Description of what kind of query will be made to the trie.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.Trie.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. A key-value datastore implemented as a database-backed modified Merkle tree.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieCache.html)- Cache
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. A cache that can be used to speed-up certain operations when accessing the trie.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieConfiguration.html)- Configuration
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. This trait associates a trie definition with preferred methods. It also contains own default implementations and can be used to allow switching implementation.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieLayout.html)- Layout
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Trait with definition of trie layout. Contains all associated trait needed for a trie definition or implementation.
- [TrieMut](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieMut.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. A key-value datastore implemented as a database-backed modified Merkle tree.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieRecorder.html)- Recorder
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. A trie recorder that can be used to record all kind of`TrieAccess`
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/trait.TrieRecorderProvider.html)- Recorder - Provider
- Type that is able to provide a `trie_db::TrieRecorder`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [child_](https://docs.rs/fn.child_delta_trie_root.html)- delta_ - trie_ - root
- Determine a child trie root given a hash DB and delta values. H is the default hasher, but a generic implementation may ignore this type parameter and use other hashers.
- [child_](https://docs.rs/fn.child_trie_root.html)- trie_ - root
- Determine a child trie root given its ordered contents, closed form. H is the default hasher, but a generic implementation may ignore this type parameter and use other hashers.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_compact.html)- compact
- Trie codec reexport, mainly child trie support for trie compact proof. Decode a compact proof.
- [delta_](https://docs.rs/fn.delta_trie_root.html)- trie_ - root
- Determine a trie root given a hash DB and delta values.
- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_child_trie_root.html)- child_ - trie_ - root
- Determine the empty child trie root.
- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_trie_root.html)- trie_ - root
- Determine the empty trie root.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_compact.html)- compact
- Trie codec reexport, mainly child trie support for trie compact proof. Encode a compact proof.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_trie_proof.html)- trie_ - proof
- Create a proof for a subset of keys in a trie.
- [prefixed_](https://docs.rs/fn.prefixed_key.html)- key
- Various re-exports from the `memory-db`crate. Derive a database key from hash value of the node (key) and the node prefix.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_child_trie_first_descendant_value.html)- child_ - trie_ - first_ - descendant_ - value
- Read the `trie_db::MerkleValue`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_child_trie_hash.html)- child_ - trie_ - hash
- Read a hash from the child trie.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_child_trie_value.html)- child_ - trie_ - value
- Read a value from the child trie.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_child_trie_value_with.html)- child_ - trie_ - value_ - with
- Read a value from the child trie with given query.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_trie_first_descendant_value.html)- trie_ - first_ - descendant_ - value
- Read the `trie_db::MerkleValue`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_trie_value.html)- trie_ - value
- Read a value from the trie.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_trie_value_with.html)- trie_ - value_ - with
- Read a value from the trie with given Query.
- [verify_](https://docs.rs/fn.verify_trie_proof.html)- trie_ - proof
- Verify a set of key-value pairs against a trie root and a proof.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [CError](https://docs.rs/type.CError.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Alias accessor to`NodeCodec`associated`Error`type from a`TrieLayout`.
- [DBValue](https://docs.rs/type.DBValue.html)
- Various re-exports from the `trie-db`crate. Database value
- [Generic](https://docs.rs/type.GenericMemoryDB.html)- MemoryDB
- Reexport from `hash_db`, with genericity set for`Hasher`trait.
- [HashDB](https://docs.rs/type.HashDB.html)
- Reexport from `hash_db`, with genericity set for`Hasher`trait.
- [Lookup](https://docs.rs/type.Lookup.html)
- Querying interface, as in `trie_db`but less generic.
- [MemoryDB](https://docs.rs/type.MemoryDB.html)
- Reexport from `hash_db`, with genericity set for`Hasher`trait. This uses a noops`KeyFunction`(key addressing must be hashed or using an encoding scheme that avoid key conflict).
- [Prefixed](https://docs.rs/type.PrefixedMemoryDB.html)- MemoryDB
- Reexport from `hash_db`, with genericity set for`Hasher`trait. This uses a`KeyFunction`for prefixing keys internally (avoiding key conflict for non random keys).
- [RawStorage](https://docs.rs/type.RawStorageProof.html)- Proof
- Raw storage proof type (just raw trie nodes).
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/type.TrieDB.html)
- Persistent trie database read-access interface for a given hasher.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/type.TrieDBBuilder.html)- Builder
- Builder for creating a `TrieDB`
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/type.TrieDBMut.html)- Mut
- Persistent trie database write-access interface for a given hasher.
- [TrieDB](https://docs.rs/type.TrieDBMutBuilder.html)- MutBuilder
- Builder for creating a `TrieDBMut`
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/type.TrieError.html)- Error
- TrieDB error over `TrieConfiguration`trait.
- [Trie](https://docs.rs/type.TrieHash.html)- Hash
- Hash type for a trie layout.

# sp-trie 46.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sp-trie/latest

Utility functions to interact with Substrate's Base-16 Modified Merkle Patricia tree ("trie").

License: Apache-2.0

# ahash - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ahash/^0.8.2/

## Expand description

AHash is a high performance keyed hash function.

It quickly provides a high quality hash where the result is not predictable without knowing the Key.
AHash works with `HashMap` to hash keys, but without allowing for the possibility that an malicious user can
induce a collision.

[§](https://docs.rs#how-ahash-works)How aHash works

When it is available aHash uses the hardware AES instructions to provide a keyed hash function. When it is not, aHash falls back on a slightly slower alternative algorithm.

Because aHash does not have a fixed standard for its output, it is able to improve over time. But this also means that different computers or computers using different versions of ahash may observe different hash values for the same input.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic Usage

AHash provides an implementation of the [Hasher] trait. To construct a HashMap using aHash as its hasher do the following:

```
use ahash::{AHasher, RandomState};
use std::collections::HashMap;
let mut map: HashMap<i32, i32, RandomState> = HashMap::default();
map.insert(12, 34);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#randomness)Randomness

The above requires a source of randomness to generate keys for the hashmap. By default this obtained from the OS.
It is also possible to have randomness supplied via the `compile-time-rng` flag, or manually.

[§](https://docs.rs#if-randomness-is-not-available)If randomness is not available

[AHasher::default()](https://docs.rs/struct.AHasher.html#method.default) can be used to hash using fixed keys. This works with
[BuildHasherDefault](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/struct.BuildHasherDefault.html). For example:

```
use std::hash::BuildHasherDefault;
use std::collections::HashMap;
use ahash::AHasher;
let mut m: HashMap<_, _, BuildHasherDefault<AHasher>> = HashMap::default();
```
It is also possible to instantiate [RandomState](https://docs.rs/random_state/struct.RandomState.html) directly:

```
use ahash::HashMap;
use ahash::RandomState;
let mut m = HashMap::with_hasher(RandomState::with_seed(42));
```
Or for uses besides a hashhmap:

```
use std::hash::BuildHasher;
use ahash::RandomState;
let hash_builder = RandomState::with_seed(42);
let hash = hash_builder.hash_one("Some Data");
```
There are several constructors for [RandomState](https://docs.rs/random_state/struct.RandomState.html) with different ways to supply seeds.

[§](https://docs.rs#convenience-wrappers)Convenience wrappers

For convenience, both new-type wrappers and type aliases are provided.

The new type wrappers are called called `AHashMap` and `AHashSet`.

```
use ahash::AHashMap;
let mut map: AHashMap<i32, i32> = AHashMap::new();
map.insert(12, 34);
```
This avoids the need to type “RandomState”. (For convenience `From`, `Into`, and `Deref` are provided).

[§](https://docs.rs#aliases)Aliases

For even less typing and better interop with existing libraries (such as rayon) which require a `std::collection::HashMap` ,
the type aliases [HashMap](https://docs.rs/type.HashMap.html), [HashSet](https://docs.rs/type.HashSet.html) are provided.

```
use ahash::{HashMap, HashMapExt};
let mut map: HashMap<i32, i32> = HashMap::new();
map.insert(12, 34);
```
Note the import of [HashMapExt](https://docs.rs/trait.HashMapExt.html). This is needed for the constructor.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::random_state::`- [RandomState](https://docs.rs/random_state/struct.RandomState.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AHash](https://docs.rs/struct.AHashMap.html)- Map
- A `HashMap``RandomState``std`feature to be enabled.)
- [AHash](https://docs.rs/struct.AHashSet.html)- Set
- A `HashSet``RandomState``std`feature to be enabled.)
- [AHasher](https://docs.rs/struct.AHasher.html)
- A `Hasher`for hashing an arbitrary stream of bytes.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Hash](https://docs.rs/trait.HashMapExt.html)- MapExt
- A convenience trait that can be used together with the type aliases defined to
get access to the `new()`and`with_capacity()`methods for the HashMap type alias.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/trait.HashSetExt.html)- SetExt
- A convenience trait that can be used together with the type aliases defined to
get access to the `new()`and`with_capacity()`methods for the HashSet type aliases.

# parity_scale_codec - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parity-scale-codec/^3.7.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#parity-scale-codec)Parity SCALE Codec

Rust implementation of the SCALE (Simple Concatenated Aggregate Little-Endian) data format for types used in the Parity Substrate framework.

SCALE is a light-weight format which allows encoding (and decoding) which makes it highly suitable for resource-constrained execution environments like blockchain runtimes and low-power, low-memory devices.

It is important to note that the encoding context (knowledge of how the types and data structures look) needs to be known separately at both encoding and decoding ends. The encoded data does not include this contextual information.

To get a better understanding of how the encoding is done for different types,
take a look at the [“Type encoding (SCALE)” page in Substrate docs](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

The codec is implemented using the following traits:

[§](https://docs.rs#encode)Encode

The `Encode` trait is used for encoding of data into the SCALE format. The `Encode` trait
contains the following functions:

- `size_hint(&self) -> usize`: Gets the capacity (in bytes) required for the encoded data. This is to avoid double-allocation of memory needed for the encoding. It can be an estimate and does not need to be an exact number. If the size is not known, even no good maximum, then we can skip this function from the trait implementation. This is required to be a cheap operation, so should not involve iterations etc.
- `encode_to<T: Output>(&self, dest: &mut T)`: Encodes the value and appends it to a destination buffer.
- `encode(&self) -> Vec<u8>`: Encodes the type data and returns a slice.
- `using_encoded<R, F: FnOnce(&[u8]) -> R>(&self, f: F) -> R`: Encodes the type data and executes a closure on the encoded value. Returns the result from the executed closure.

**Note:** Implementations should override `using_encoded` for value types and `encode_to` for
allocating types. `size_hint` should be implemented for all types, wherever possible. Wrapper
types should override all methods.

[§](https://docs.rs#decode)Decode

The `Decode` trait is used for deserialization/decoding of encoded data into the respective
types.

- `fn decode<I: Input>(value: &mut I) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Tries to decode the value from SCALE format to the type it is called on. Returns an- `Err`if the decoding fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#compactas)CompactAs

The `CompactAs` trait is used for wrapping custom types/structs as compact types, which makes
them even more space/memory efficient. The compact encoding is described [here](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/scale-codec/#fn-1).

- `encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As`: Encodes the type (self) as a compact type. The type- `As`is defined in the same trait and its implementation should be compact encode-able.
- `decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error>`: Decodes the type (self) from a compact encode-able type.

[§](https://docs.rs#hascompact)HasCompact

The `HasCompact` trait, if implemented, tells that the corresponding type is a compact
encode-able type.

[§](https://docs.rs#encodelike)EncodeLike

The `EncodeLike` trait needs to be implemented for each type manually. When using derive, it is
done automatically for you. Basically the trait gives you the opportunity to accept multiple
types to a function that all encode to the same representation.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples)Usage Examples

Following are some examples to demonstrate usage of the codec.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-types)Simple types

```
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
enum EnumType {
    #[codec(index = 15)]
    A,
    B(u32, u64),
    C {
        a: u32,
        b: u64,
    },
}
let a = EnumType::A;
let b = EnumType::B(1, 2);
let c = EnumType::C { a: 1, b: 2 };
a.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x0f");
});
b.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0");
});
c.using_encoded(|ref slice| {
    assert_eq!(slice, &b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0");
});
let mut da: &[u8] = b"\x0f";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut da).ok(), Some(a));
let mut db: &[u8] = b"\x01\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut db).ok(), Some(b));
let mut dc: &[u8] = b"\x02\x01\0\0\0\x02\0\0\0\0\0\0\0";
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut dc).ok(), Some(c));
let mut dz: &[u8] = &[0];
assert_eq!(EnumType::decode(&mut dz).ok(), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compact-type-with-hascompact)Compact type with HasCompact

```
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode, Compact, HasCompact};
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
struct Test1CompactHasCompact<T: HasCompact> {
    #[codec(compact)]
    bar: T,
}
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
struct Test1HasCompact<T: HasCompact> {
    #[codec(encoded_as = "<T as HasCompact>::Type")]
    bar: T,
}
let test_val: (u64, usize) = (0u64, 1usize);
let encoded = Test1HasCompact { bar: test_val.0 }.encode();
assert_eq!(encoded.len(), test_val.1);
assert_eq!(<Test1CompactHasCompact<u64>>::decode(&mut &encoded[..]).unwrap().bar, test_val.0);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#type-with-compactas)Type with CompactAs

```
use serde_derive::{Serialize, Deserialize};
use parity_scale_codec::{Encode, Decode, Compact, HasCompact, CompactAs, Error};
#[cfg_attr(feature = "std", derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug))]
#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
struct StructHasCompact(u32);
impl CompactAs for StructHasCompact {
    type As = u32;
    fn encode_as(&self) -> &Self::As {
        &12
    }
    fn decode_from(_: Self::As) -> Result<Self, Error> {
        Ok(StructHasCompact(12))
    }
}
impl From<Compact<StructHasCompact>> for StructHasCompact {
    fn from(_: Compact<StructHasCompact>) -> Self {
        StructHasCompact(12)
    }
}
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Encode, Decode)]
enum TestGenericHasCompact<T> {
    A {
        #[codec(compact)] a: T
    },
}
let a = TestGenericHasCompact::A::<StructHasCompact> {
    a: StructHasCompact(12325678),
};
let encoded = a.encode();
assert_eq!(encoded.len(), 2);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#derive-attributes)Derive attributes

The derive implementation supports the following attributes:

- `codec(dumb_trait_bound)`: This attribute needs to be placed above the type that one of the trait should be implemented for. It will make the algorithm that determines the to-add trait bounds fall back to just use the type parameters of the type. This can be useful for situation where the algorithm includes private types in the public interface. By using this attribute, you should not get this error/warning again.
- `codec(skip)`: Needs to be placed above a field or variant and makes it to be skipped while encoding/decoding.
- `codec(compact)`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field use compact encoding. (The type needs to support compact encoding.)
- `codec(encoded_as = "OtherType")`: Needs to be placed above a field and makes the field being encoded by using- `OtherType`.
- `codec(index = 0)`: Needs to be placed above an enum variant to make the variant use the given index when encoded. By default the index is determined by counting from- `0`beginning wth the first variant.
- `codec(encode_bound)`,- `codec(decode_bound)`and- `codec(mel_bound)`: All 3 attributes take in a- `where`clause for the- `Encode`,- `Decode`and- `MaxEncodedLen`trait implementation for the annotated type respectively.
- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params))`,- `codec(decode_bound(skip_type_params))`and- `codec(mel_bound(skip_type_params))`: All 3 sub-attributes take in types as arguments to skip trait derivation of the corresponding trait, e.g. T in- `codec(encode_bound(skip_type_params(T)))`will not contain a- `Encode`trait bound while- `Encode`is being derived for the annotated type.

[§](https://docs.rs#known-issues)Known issues

Even though this crate supports deserialization of arbitrarily sized array (e.g. `[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]`)
using such types is not recommended and will most likely result in a stack overflow. If you have a big
array inside of your structure which you want to decode you should wrap it in a `Box`, e.g. `Box<[T; 1024 * 1024 * 1024]>`.

License: Apache-2.0

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.Compact.html)
- Compact-encoded variant of T. This is more space-efficient but less compute-efficient.
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/struct.CompactRef.html)- Ref
- Compact-encoded variant of &’a T. This is more space-efficient but less compute-efficient.
- [Counted](https://docs.rs/struct.CountedInput.html)- Input
- A wrapper for `Input`which tracks the number fo bytes that are successfully read.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/struct.DecodeFinished.html)- Finished
- A zero-sized type signifying that the decoding finished.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error type.
- [IoReader](https://docs.rs/struct.IoReader.html)
- Wrapper that implements Input for any `Read`type.
- [MemTracking](https://docs.rs/struct.MemTrackingInput.html)- Input
- `Input`implementation that can be used for limiting the heap memory usage while decoding.
- [Option](https://docs.rs/struct.OptionBool.html)- Bool
- Shim type because we can’t do a specialised implementation for `Option<bool>`directly.
- [Ref](https://docs.rs/struct.Ref.html)
- Reference wrapper that implement encode like any type that is encoded like its inner type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Codec](https://docs.rs/trait.Codec.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy read/write of value-references to/from slices in LE format.
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/trait.CompactAs.html)- As
- Allow foreign structs to be wrap in Compact
- [Compact](https://docs.rs/trait.CompactLen.html)- Len
- Something that can return the compact encoded length for a given value.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.Decode.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy read of value-references from slices in LE format.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeAll.html)- All
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeLength.html)- Length
- Trait that allows the length of a collection to be read, without having to read and decode the entire elements.
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeLimit.html)- Limit
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeWithMemLimit.html)- With - MemLimit
- Extension trait to `Decode`
- [Decode](https://docs.rs/trait.DecodeWithMemTracking.html)- With - MemTracking
- Marker trait used for identifying types that call the `Input::on_before_alloc_mem`
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.Encode.html)
- Trait that allows zero-copy write of value-references to slices in LE format.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeAppend.html)- Append
- Trait that allows to append items to an encoded representation without decoding all previous added items.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeAsRef.html)- AsRef
- Something that can be encoded as a reference.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/trait.EncodeLike.html)- Like
- A marker trait that tells the compiler that a type encode to the same representation as another type.
- [Full](https://docs.rs/trait.FullCodec.html)- Codec
- Trait that bound `EncodeLike`along with`Codec`. Usefull for generic being used in function with`EncodeLike`parameters.
- [Full](https://docs.rs/trait.FullEncode.html)- Encode
- Trait that bound `EncodeLike`along with`Encode`. Usefull for generic being used in function with`EncodeLike`parameters.
- [HasCompact](https://docs.rs/trait.HasCompact.html)
- Trait that tells you if a given type can be encoded/decoded in a compact way.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/trait.Input.html)
- Trait that allows reading of data into a slice.
- [Joiner](https://docs.rs/trait.Joiner.html)
- Trait to allow itself to be serialised into a value which can be extended by bytes.
- [Keyed](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyedVec.html)- Vec
- Trait to allow itself to be serialised and prepended by a given slice.
- [Output](https://docs.rs/trait.Output.html)
- Trait that allows writing of data.
- [Wrapper](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapperTypeDecode.html)- Type - Decode
- A marker trait for types that can be created solely from other decodable types.
- [Wrapper](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapperTypeEncode.html)- Type - Encode
- A marker trait for types that wrap other encodable type.

# foldhash - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/foldhash/^0.1.5/

## Expand description

This crate provides foldhash, a fast, non-cryptographic, minimally DoS-resistant hashing algorithm designed for computational uses such as hashmaps, bloom filters, count sketching, etc.

When should you **not** use foldhash:

-
You are afraid of people studying your long-running program’s behavior to reverse engineer its internal random state and using this knowledge to create many colliding inputs for computational complexity attacks.
-
You expect foldhash to have a consistent output across versions or platforms, such as for persistent file formats or communication protocols.
-
You are relying on foldhash’s properties for any kind of security. Foldhash is **not appropriate for any cryptographic purpose**.

Foldhash has two variants, one optimized for speed which is ideal for data
structures such as hash maps and bloom filters, and one optimized for
statistical quality which is ideal for algorithms such as
[HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog) and
[MinHash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MinHash).

Foldhash can be used in a `#![no_std]` environment by disabling its default
`"std"` feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The easiest way to use this crate with the standard library [ HashMap](https://docs.rs/type.HashMap.html) or

[is to import them from](https://docs.rs/type.HashSet.html)

`HashSet``foldhash` instead, along with the
extension traits to make [and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html#method.new)

`HashMap::new`[work out-of-the-box:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html#method.with_capacity)

`HashMap::with_capacity````
use foldhash::{HashMap, HashMapExt};
let mut hm = HashMap::new();
hm.insert(42, "hello");
```
You can also avoid the convenience types and do it manually by initializing
a [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/fast/struct.RandomState.html), for example if you are using a different hash map
implementation like

[:](https://docs.rs/hashbrown/)

`hashbrown````
use hashbrown::HashMap;
use foldhash::fast::RandomState;
let mut hm = HashMap::with_hasher(RandomState::default());
hm.insert("foo", "bar");
```
The above methods are the recommended way to use foldhash, which will
automatically generate a randomly generated hasher instance for you. If you
absolutely must have determinism you can use [ FixedState](https://docs.rs/fast/struct.FixedState.html)
instead, but note that this makes you trivially vulnerable to HashDoS
attacks and might lead to quadratic runtime when moving data from one
hashmap/set into another:

```
use std::collections::HashSet;
use foldhash::fast::FixedState;
let mut hm = HashSet::with_hasher(FixedState::with_seed(42));
hm.insert([1, 10, 100]);
```
If you rely on statistical properties of the hash for the correctness of
your algorithm, such as in [HyperLogLog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HyperLogLog),
it is suggested to use the [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.RandomState.html)
or

[from the](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.FixedState.html)

`FixedState`[module instead of the](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)

`quality`[module. The latter is optimized purely for speed in hash tables and has known statistical imperfections.](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)

`fast`Finally, you can also directly use the [ RandomState](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.RandomState.html)
or

[to manually hash items using the](https://docs.rs/quality/struct.FixedState.html)

`FixedState`[trait:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)

`BuildHasher````
use std::hash::BuildHasher;
use foldhash::quality::RandomState;
let random_state = RandomState::default();
let hash = random_state.hash_one("hello world");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#seeding)Seeding

Foldhash relies on a single 8-byte per-hasher seed which should be ideally
be different from each instance to instance, and also a larger
[ SharedSeed](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedSeed.html) which may be shared by many different instances.

To reduce overhead, this [ SharedSeed](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedSeed.html) is typically initialized once and
stored. To prevent each hashmap unnecessarily containing a reference to this
value there are three kinds of

[s foldhash provides (both for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/hash/trait.BuildHasher.html)

`BuildHasher`[and](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)

`fast`[):](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)

`quality`- `RandomState`- `SharedSeed::global_random`
- `FixedState`- `SharedSeed::global_fixed`
- `SeedableRandomState`- `RandomState`- `SharedSeed`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [fast](https://docs.rs/fast/index.html)
- The foldhash implementation optimized for speed.
- [quality](https://docs.rs/quality/index.html)
- The foldhash implementation optimized for quality.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Shared](https://docs.rs/struct.SharedSeed.html)- Seed
- A random seed intended to be shared by many different foldhash instances.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Hash](https://docs.rs/trait.HashMapExt.html)- MapExt
- A convenience extension trait to enable `HashMap::new``foldhash`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/trait.HashSetExt.html)- SetExt
- A convenience extension trait to enable `HashSet::new``foldhash`.

# hash_db - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hash-db/^0.16.0/

## Expand description

Database of byte-slices keyed to their hash.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [EMPTY_](https://docs.rs/static.EMPTY_PREFIX.html)- PREFIX
- An empty prefix constant. Can be use when the prefix is not use internally or for root nodes.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsHashDB](https://docs.rs/trait.AsHashDB.html)
- Upcast trait for HashDB.
- [AsPlainDB](https://docs.rs/trait.AsPlainDB.html)
- Upcast trait for PlainDB.
- [HashDB](https://docs.rs/trait.HashDB.html)
- Trait modelling datastore keyed by a hash defined by the `Hasher`.
- [HashDB](https://docs.rs/trait.HashDBRef.html)- Ref
- Trait for immutable reference of HashDB.
- [Hasher](https://docs.rs/trait.Hasher.html)
- Trait describing an object that can hash a slice of bytes. Used to abstract
other types over the hashing algorithm. Defines a single `hash`method and an`Out`associated type with the necessary bounds.
- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/trait.MaybeDebug.html)- Debug
- [PlainDB](https://docs.rs/trait.PlainDB.html)
- Trait modelling a plain datastore whose key is a fixed type. The caller should ensure that a key only corresponds to one value.
- [PlainDB](https://docs.rs/trait.PlainDBRef.html)- Ref
- Trait for immutable reference of PlainDB.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/type.Prefix.html)
- A trie node prefix, it is the nibble path from the trie root to the trie node. For a node containing no partial key value it is the full key. For a value node or node containing a partial key, it is the full key minus its node partial nibbles (the node key can be split into prefix and node partial). Therefore it is always the leftmost portion of the node key, so its internal representation is a non expanded byte slice followed by a last padded byte representation. The padded byte is an optional padded value.

# hashbrown - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hashbrown/^0.15.3/

## Expand description

This crate is a Rust port of Google’s high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash
map, adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust’s standard `HashMap`
and `HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_map/index.html)- map
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_set/index.html)- set
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.

# parking_lot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parking_lot/^0.12.1/

## Expand description

This library provides implementations of `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Condvar` and
`Once` that are smaller, faster and more flexible than those in the Rust
standard library. It also provides a `ReentrantMutex` type.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ArcReentrant](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcReentrantMutexGuard.html)- Mutex - Guard

- [ArcRw](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcRwLockReadGuard.html)- Lock - Read - Guard
- An RAII rwlock guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`RwLock`.
- [ArcRw](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcRwLockUpgradableReadGuard.html)- Lock - Upgradable - Read - Guard
- An RAII rwlock guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`RwLock`. This is similar to the`RwLockUpgradableReadGuard`struct, except instead of using a reference to unlock the`RwLock`it uses an`Arc<RwLock>`. This has several advantages, most notably that it has an`'static`lifetime.

- [RawMutex](https://docs.rs/struct.RawMutex.html)

# substrate_prometheus_endpoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/substrate-prometheus-endpoint/^0.17.7/

A Metric counts individual observations from an event or sample stream
in configurable buckets. Similar to a Summary,
it also provides a sum of observations and an observation count.

A struct that bundles the options for creating a Histogram metric. It is
mandatory to set Name and Help to a non-empty string. All other fields are
optional and can safely be left at their zero value.

Create count buckets, where the lowest bucket has an
upper bound of start and each following bucket’s upper bound is factor
times the previous bucket’s upper bound. The final +Inf bucket is not counted
and not included in the returned slice. The returned slice is meant to be
used for the Buckets field of HistogramOpts.

Create count buckets, each width wide, where the lowest
bucket has an upper bound of start. The final +Inf bucket is not counted
and not included in the returned slice. The returned slice is meant to be
used for the Buckets field of HistogramOpts.

A Collector that bundles a set of Histograms that all share the
same Desc, but have different values for their variable labels. This is used
if you want to count the same thing partitioned by various dimensions
(e.g. HTTP request latencies, partitioned by status code and method).

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

# scale_info - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/scale-info/^2.11.6/

## Expand description

Efficient and space-efficient serialization of Rust types.

This library provides structures to easily retrieve compile-time type
information at runtime and also to serialize this information in a
space-efficient form, aka `PortableForm`.

[§](https://docs.rs#registry)Registry

At the heart of its functionality is the [ Registry](https://docs.rs/struct.Registry.html)
that acts as a cache for known types in order to efficiently deduplicate
types and ensure a space-efficient serialization.

[§](https://docs.rs#type-information)Type Information

Information about types is provided via the [ TypeInfo](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeInfo.html)
trait.

This trait should be implemented for all types that are serializable.
`scale-info` provides implementations for all commonly used Rust standard
types and a derive macro for implementing of custom types.

[§](https://docs.rs#deriving-typeinfo)Deriving `TypeInfo`

Enable the `derive` feature of this crate:

`scale-info = { version = "2.0.0", features = ["derive"] }`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use scale_info::TypeInfo;
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
struct MyStruct {
    a: u32,
    b: MyEnum,
}
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
enum MyEnum {
    A(bool),
    B { f: Vec<u8> },
    C,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

[§](https://docs.rs#scale_infobounds)`#[scale_info(bounds(..))]`

Replace the auto-generated `where` clause bounds for the derived `TypeInfo` implementation.

The derive macro automatically adds `TypeInfo` bounds for all type parameters, and all field
types containing type parameters or associated types.

This is naive and sometimes adds unnecessary bounds, since on a syntactical level there is no way to differentiate between a generic type constructor and a type alias with a generic argument e.g.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
trait MyTrait {
    type A;
}
type MyAlias<T> = <T as MyTrait>::A;
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
struct MyStruct<T> {
    a: MyAlias<T>,
    b: Vec<T>,
}
```
So for the above, since a `MyAlias<T>: TypeInfo` bound is required, and we can’t distinguish
between `MyAlias<T>` and `Vec<T>`, then the `TypeInfo` bound is simply added for all
fields which contain any type param. In this case the redundant `Vec<T>: TypeInfo`
would be added.

This is usually okay, but in some circumstances can cause problems, for example with the
[`overflow evaluating the requirement`] error [here](https://github.com/paritytech/scale-info/blob/master/test_suite/tests/ui/pass_custom_bounds_fix_overflow.rs).

The `bounds` attribute provides an [“escape hatch”](https://serde.rs/attr-bound.html) to allow
the programmer control of the `where` clause on the generated `impl`, to solve this and other
issues that can’t be foreseen by the auto-generated bounds heuristic.

[§](https://docs.rs#scale_infoskip_type_params)`#[scale_info(skip_type_params(..))]`

Remove the requirement for the specified type params to implement `TypeInfo`.

Consider a simple example of a type parameter which is used for associated types, but the type itself does not carry any type information. Consider this common pattern:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
trait Config {
    type Balance;
}
struct Runtime; // doesn't implement `TypeInfo`
impl Config for Runtime {
    type Balance = u64;
}
#[allow(unused)]
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
#[scale_info(skip_type_params(T))]
struct A<T: Config> {
    balance: T::Balance,
    marker: core::marker::PhantomData<T>,
}
fn assert_type_info<T: scale_info::TypeInfo + 'static>() {}
fn main() {
    // without the `skip_type_params` attribute this will fail.
    assert_type_info::<A<Runtime>>();
}
```
By default, the derived `TypeInfo` implementation will add the type of all type parameters to
the `TypeParameter` specification e.g.

`type_params(vec![TypeParameter::new("T", Some(MetaType::new::<T>()))])`

In the example above, this will cause a compiler error because `Runtime` is the concrete tyoe
for `T`, which does not satisfy the `TypeInfo` requirement of `MetaType::new::<T>()`.

Simply adding a `TypeInfo` derive to `Runtime` is one way of solving this, but that could be
misleading (why does it need `TypeInfo` if a value of that type is never encoded?), and can
sometimes require adding `TypeInfo` bounds in other impl blocks.

The `skip_type_params` attribute solves this, providing an additional “escape hatch” which
prevents the given type parameter’s type information being required:

`type_params(vec![TypeParameter::new("T", None)])`

The generated type params do not now require `T` to implement `TypeInfo`, so the auto-generated
bound is not added to the generated `TypeInfo` `where` clause.

[§](https://docs.rs#combining-bounds-and-skip_type_params)Combining `bounds` and `skip_type_params`

These two attributes can complement one another, particularly in the case where using `bounds`
would still require manually adding a `TypeInfo` bound for the type parameter:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
#[scale_info(bounds(), skip_type_params(T))]
struct A<T> {
    marker: core::marker::PhantomData<T>,
}
```
Without `skip_type_params` in the example above, it would require the `TypeInfo` bounds for `T`
to be added manually e.g. `#[scale_info(bounds(T: TypeInfo + 'static))]`. Since the intention of
the empty bounds is to **remove** all type bounds, then the addition of `skip_type_params`
allows this to compile successfully.

[§](https://docs.rs#precedence)Precedence

When used independently, both attributes modify the `where` clause of the derived `TypeInfo`
impl. When used together, the predicates supplied in the `bounds` attribute replaces *all*
auto-generated bounds, and `skip_type_params` will have no effect on the resulting `where`
clause.

**Note:** When using `bounds` without `skip_type_params`, it is therefore required to manually
add a `TypeInfo` bound for any non skipped type parameters. The compiler will let you know.

[§](https://docs.rs#scale_infocapture_docs--defaultalwaysnever)`#[scale_info(capture_docs = "default|always|never")]`

Docs for types, fields and variants can all be captured by the `docs` feature being enabled.
This can be overridden using the `capture_docs` attribute:

`#[scale_info(capture_docs = "default")]` will capture docs iff the `docs` feature is enabled.
This is the default if `capture_docs` is not specified.

`#[scale_info(capture_docs = "always")]` will capture docs for the annotated type even if the
`docs` feature is *not* enabled.

`#[scale_info(capture_docs = "never")]` will *not* capture docs for the annotated type even if
the `docs` is enabled.

This is useful e.g. when compiling metadata into a Wasm blob, and it is desirable to keep the
binary size as small as possible, so the `docs` feature would be disabled. In case the docs for
some types is necessary they could be enabled on a per-type basis with the above attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#scale_infocrate--pathtocrate)`#[scale_info(crate = path::to::crate)]`

Specify a path to the scale-info crate instance to use when referring to the APIs from generated code. This is normally only applicable when invoking re-exported scale-info derives from a public macro in a different crate. For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use scale_info_reexport::info::TypeInfo;
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
#[scale_info(crate = scale_info_reexport::info)]
enum TestEnum {
    FirstVariant,
    SecondVariant,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#scale_inforeplace_segmentsearch-replace)`#[scale_info(replace_segment("search", "replace"))]`

Specify to rename a segment in the `path` returned by the [`TypeInfo::path`] function.
Normally the path is generated by using the `module_path!` macro. This path includes
the crate name and all the modules up to the declaration of the type. Sometimes it
is useful to replace one of these segments to ensure that for example a renaming
of the crate isn’t propagated to downstream users. Be aware that if a `crate-name`
contains an hypen, the actual segment is `crate_name`. The `replace` name needs
to be a valid Rust identifier. The attribute is allowed to be passed multiple
times to replace multiple segments.

Example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use scale_info_reexport::info::TypeInfo;
#[derive(TypeInfo)]
#[scale_info(replace_segment("something", "better_name"))]
#[scale_info(replace_segment("TestEnum", "BetterEnumName"))]
enum TestEnum {
    FirstVariant,
    SecondVariant,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#forms)Forms

To bridge between compile-time type information and runtime the
[ MetaForm](https://docs.rs/form/enum.MetaForm.html) is used to easily retrieve all
information needed to uniquely identify types.

The `MetaForm` and its associated `Registry` can be transformed into the
space-efficient form by the [ IntoPortable](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoPortable.html) trait; it is
used internally by the

[in order to convert the expanded types into their space-efficient form.](https://docs.rs/struct.Registry.html)

`Registry`[§](https://docs.rs#symbols-and-namespaces)Symbols and Namespaces

To differentiate two types sharing the same name, namespaces are used.
Commonly the namespace is equal to the one where the type has been defined
in. For Rust prelude types such as [ Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html) and

[the root namespace (empty namespace) is used.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`To use this library simply use the [ MetaForm](https://docs.rs/form/enum.MetaForm.html)
initially with your own data structures; make them generic over the

[trait just as has been done in this crate with](https://docs.rs/form/trait.Form.html)

`Form`[in order to get a simple implementation of](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeInfo.html)

`TypeInfo`[. Use a single instance of the](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoPortable.html)

`IntoPortable`[for compaction and provide this registry instance upon serialization.](https://docs.rs/struct.Registry.html)

`Registry`A usage example can be found in ink! here: https://github.com/paritytech/ink/blob/master/abi/src/specs.rs

# schnellru - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/schnellru/^0.2.3/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#a-fast-and-flexible-lru-map)A fast and flexible LRU map

This repository contains a fast and flexible LRU map.

- Blazingly fast. Up to twice as fast as the `lru`
- Can be also used as an ordered map, with roughly the same performance as `indexmap``indexmap`only supports O(n) non-perturbing removals).
- Customizable. Out-of-box can be limited by length or by memory usage, but supports custom limiters which can be made to limit the map by whatever you want.
- Tested, miri-clean, clippy-clean and fuzzed.
- Supports `no_std`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use schnellru::{LruMap, ByLength};
let mut map = LruMap::new(ByLength::new(3));
// Insert three elements.
map.insert(1, "one");
map.insert(2, "two");
map.insert(3, "three");
assert_eq!(map.len(), 3);
// They're ordered according to which one was inserted last.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&2, &"two"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
// Access the least recently inserted one.
assert_eq!(*map.get(&1).unwrap(), "one");
// Now the order's changed.
// The element we've accessed was moved to the front.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&2, &"two"));
// Insert a fourth element.
// This will automatically pop the least recently accessed one.
map.insert(4, "four");
// Still the same number of elements.
assert_eq!(map.len(), 3);
// And this is the one which was removed.
assert!(map.peek(&2).is_none());
// And here's the new order.
let mut iter = map.iter();
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&4, &"four"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&1, &"one"));
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), (&3, &"three"));
```
